claim: For New York City resident income tax, New York City is the five boroughs: the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island. On state forms the boroughs are entered by county name: Bronx, Kings (Brooklyn), New York (Manhattan), Queens and Richmond (Staten Island). Brooklyn, Queens, Manhattan and the Bronx are all inside NYC for the resident tax.
establishes: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance (DTF): 'New York City includes the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island.' NYC residents report the city tax on Form IT-201. The county-name mapping comes from a DTF search snippet of the IT-201 instructions, not a page that was read in full.
uncertainty: None on the borough list. The county-name mapping was read in a search snippet only.
designImplication: A resident of any of the five boroughs owes the NYC resident tax. Brooklyn, Queens, Manhattan, the Bronx and Staten Island should not be modelled as separate tax jurisdictions.

claim: A person is an NYC resident if NYC is their domicile, or if they keep a permanent place of abode in NYC for substantially all of the year and spend 184 days or more there. Any part of a day counts as a day. DTF applies the state definitions to the city by putting 'New York City' in place of 'New York State'.
establishes: DTF income tax definitions page: a resident is someone whose domicile is in the state, or who maintains 'a permanent place of abode ... for substantially all of the taxable year and spend[s] 184 days or more' there. The page says the same definitions apply to NYC.
uncertainty: The page does not define 'substantially all'.
designImplication: Residence is a status (domicile, or abode plus 184 days), not just where the person sleeps on 1 January. A move into or out of the five boroughs makes the person a part-year resident.

claim: For tax year 2026 the NYC resident tax on single and married-filing-separately filers is graduated: 3.078% of taxable income up to $12,000; $369 plus 3.762% of the excess over $12,000, up to $25,000; $858 plus 3.819% of the excess over $25,000, up to $50,000; and $1,813 plus 3.876% of the excess over $50,000.
sourceDate: IT-2105-I (2026), page 10; accessed 2026-10-11; applies to tax year 2026
establishes: The NYC tax rate schedule on page 10 of DTF's 2026 estimated-tax instructions (IT-2105-I), extracted from the PDF text. The joint and head-of-household brackets use the same rates: joint $21,600/$45,000/$90,000, head of household $14,400/$30,000/$60,000.
uncertainty: These are the estimated-tax instructions, not the 2026 IT-201 instructions, which had not been published when this was accessed. Secondary reports (forvismazars, cbiz, BDO) say the FY2027 state budget, signed 2026-05-28, left personal income tax rates unchanged. The Senate and Assembly declined the mayor's proposed extra 2 points on income over $1M (secondary: abc7ny, nysfocus).
designImplication: Model NYC as a four-bracket graduated tax on NY taxable income, computed on the state return. The top rate of 3.876% starts at only $50,000 for a single filer.

claim: The 2025 NYC rate schedule for single filers is identical to 2026: 3.078% up to $12,000; $369 + 3.762% to $25,000; $858 + 3.819% to $50,000; $1,813 + 3.876% over $50,000. No official 2027 schedule was found.
establishes: The 'New York City tax rate schedule' in DTF's 2025 IT-201 instructions. Returns with NYC taxable income under $65,000 use the NYC tax table instead.
uncertainty: 2027: NOT FOUND. No official 2027 schedule has been published.
designImplication: Hold the NYC schedule constant for 2025 and 2026. For 2027, carry it forward only as an explicit assumption.

claim: NYC resident tax is not a separate return. It is computed and reported on the New York State resident return, Form IT-201, which is due April 15. The 2026 estimated tax instalments are due April 15, June 15 and September 15, 2026 and January 15, 2027.
establishes: DTF: 'You must report your New York City resident income tax ... on Form IT-201'. The instalment dates are from the IT-2105-I (2026) text.
uncertainty: The April 15 annual due date was not quoted from a page read in full. It is the IT-2105-I first-instalment date and the state return date.
designImplication: One filing event covers state and city. Treat NYC tax as an extra line on the state return, not a second return.

claim: Employers withhold NYC resident tax from NYC residents' wages alongside state withholding, using DTF's NYC withholding tables (publication NYS-50-T-NYC).
sourceDate: publication located by search; contents not read; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DTF publishes NYC-specific withholding tables, NYS-50-T-NYC, alongside the state tables, NYS-50-T-NYS (1/26).
uncertainty: The contents of NYS-50-T-NYC were not read. Its existence and title come from DTF search results.
designImplication: Withhold NYC tax through payroll for residents, then reconcile on the state return.

claim: DTF's penalties apply to NYC tax because it is on the state return. Late filing costs 5% of the tax due for each month or part of a month, up to 25%. A return more than 60 days late has a minimum penalty of the lesser of $100 or the total amount due. Late payment costs 0.5% of the unpaid amount per month or part of a month, up to 25%. Interest is compounded daily at a rate DTF sets each quarter. The underpayment rate for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is 9.5%.
sourceDate: page updated 2025-10-23; Q4 2026 rate from https://www.tax.ny.gov/pay/interest/2026/p4.htm (released 2026-08-20); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: DTF interest and penalties page, and DTF's interest rate release for 10/1/26 to 12/31/26: 'the underpayment rate for this period is 9.5%'.
uncertainty: The other 2026 quarters were seen only in search snippets: Q1 9.5%, Q2 8.5%. 2027 rates: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: A late NYC balance takes the state's penalty schedule, since there is no separate city penalty.

claim: DTF collects NYC tax. An unpaid balance can lead to a tax warrant, which is filed with the Department of State and the county clerk. The warrant becomes a public record, works like a civil judgment and creates a lien on real and personal property. Next comes an income execution, which asks the person for up to 10% of gross wages and then has the employer deduct it, and then levies. An installment payment agreement (IPA) can be requested online for balances of $20,000 or less with 36 or fewer monthly payments. Penalty and interest keep accruing during an IPA, and the warrant stays on file.

value.collector: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance
steps: income execution (up to 10% of gross wages)

establishes: DTF pages on tax warrants (https://www.tax.ny.gov/enforcement/collections/tax-warrants.htm), income executions (https://www.tax.ny.gov/enforcement/collections/income-executions.htm) and IPAs, as summarised in DTF search results.
uncertainty: These facts come from search-result summaries of DTF pages. The pages themselves were not read in full.
designImplication: For an NYC debt, the escalation path is warrant, then wage execution (10%), then levy. A small balance can be cleared on a 36-month plan that does not stop interest.

claim: Nonresidents who work in NYC owe no NYC income tax. The NYC nonresident earnings tax (the 'commuter tax') was repealed effective 1 July 1999. The one exception is NYC government employees hired on or after 4 January 1973 who live outside the city: under City Charter section 1127 they must file Form NYC-1127 and pay an amount equal to the NYC resident tax they would owe.

value.exception: NYC employees hired on/after 1973-01-04 living outside NYC file NYC-1127

establishes: NYC Department of Finance: an NYC employee who lives outside the city 'must file Form NYC-1127 and pay the City an amount equal to the personal income tax you would owe if you lived in New York City.' The repeal date is from the legislative findings in NY Senate bill S3044 (2015) (https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2015/2015-s3044), citing City of New York v. State of New York, 94 NY2d 577 (2000).
uncertainty: The repeal date was read from a bill's legislative findings, not from the repealing statute (L.1999 ch.5). The NYC-1127 facts are from a search summary of the DOF FAQ page.
designImplication: An NYC tax hits residents only, wherever they work. A commuter from outside the city pays nothing to NYC unless they are a city employee.

claim: Philadelphia Wage Tax and Earnings Tax rates on gross compensation, by fiscal-year period starting 1 July. 1 July 2023 to 30 June 2025: resident 3.75%, nonresident 3.44%. 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026: resident 3.74%, nonresident 3.43%. 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027: resident 3.735%, nonresident 3.425%. 1 July 2027 to 30 June 2028: resident 3.73%, nonresident 3.42%. 1 July 2028 to 30 June 2029: resident 3.72%, nonresident 3.41%.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11; effective 1 July each year
establishes: Philadelphia Department of Revenue tax rate history page, e.g. 'July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027: 3.73500% on gross wages' for residents. The Earnings Tax page (https://www.phila.gov/services/payments-assistance-taxes/taxes/income-taxes/earnings-tax-employees/) confirms the 2025 and 2026 rows.
uncertainty: The 2027 and 2028 rows are scheduled cuts under the five-year plan Council approved in June 2025. They are published as scheduled, and Council could change them.
designImplication: The rate changes mid calendar year (1 July), so a calendar year of wages is taxed at two rates. Pay dates before 1 July take the old rate.

claim: Net Profits Tax (self-employment and business profits of individuals) is set by calendar tax year. 2023 to 2024: resident 3.75%, nonresident 3.44%. 2025: 3.74% / 3.43%. 2026: 3.735% / 3.425%. 2027: 3.73% / 3.42%. 2028: 3.72% / 3.41%. Returns are due 15 April. Estimated payments are two instalments, each 25% of the prior year's tax, due 15 April and 15 June. A return must be filed even if the business made a loss.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11; rates per tax (calendar) year
establishes: Philadelphia Revenue NPT page (2025: 'Residents: 3.74% ... Non-residents: 3.43%', due April 15, 2026) and the tax rate history page for the other years.
uncertainty: NPT runs on the calendar year, but the Wage Tax changes on 1 July.
designImplication: Self-employed Philadelphians pay NPT on calendar-year profit at one rate per year. Don't apply the Wage Tax's July split to them.

claim: A resident whose employer does not withhold the City Wage Tax (for example an out-of-state employer) must pay the Earnings Tax. They register on the Philadelphia Tax Center for an Earnings Tax account, pay quarterly and file an annual reconciliation due April 15. The 2026 quarterly due dates are April 30, July 31, October 31 and February 1, 2027. The amount is self-assessed on the return at the Earnings Tax rate, which equals the Wage Tax rate. Revenue then sends a notice with any penalty and interest.

value.whoFiles: residents (and nonresidents working in the city) without City Wage Tax withheld

establishes: Philadelphia Revenue: 'You must pay the Earnings Tax if you are a Philadelphia resident with taxable income who doesn't have the City Wage Tax withheld from your paycheck' or 'a non-resident who works in Philadelphia and doesn't have the City Wage Tax withheld.' The annual reconciliation is 'due by April 15'.
uncertainty: No page was found describing an assessment notice step specific to the Earnings Tax. The account is self-assessed and then billed under the general interest and penalty rules. A resident whose employer withholds the Wage Tax files no city return for wages.
designImplication: A resident with withholding files nothing for wages. A resident without withholding self-assesses each quarter and reconciles by April 15.

claim: Residents pay the School Income Tax (SIT) on certain unearned income: dividends, short-term capital gains, rental income, royalties, S-corporation and limited-partnership income, gambling gains, some interest and others. The 2025 rate is 3.74%. Returns are due April 15.
establishes: Philadelphia Revenue SIT page: 'Philadelphia residents who receive certain types of unearned income must pay School Income Tax (SIT).'
uncertainty: 2026 rate: NOT FOUND on the SIT page. A phila.gov search summary gave 3.735% for 2026, but it was not confirmed on a page that was read.
designImplication: Investment and rental income of residents needs its own city tax line, separate from wages.

claim: Every Pennsylvania employer of a Philadelphia resident, or of a nonresident who performs services for an employer in Philadelphia, must register with the City within 30 days and withhold the Wage Tax. Deposit frequency depends on the monthly amount withheld: under $350 is quarterly, $350 to $16,000 is monthly, and over $16,000 is semi-monthly or weekly. The 2026 quarterly due dates are April 30, July 31, October 31 and February 1, 2027. Annual reconciliations are no longer required: the fourth quarter counts as the final reconciliation.
establishes: Philadelphia Revenue Wage Tax (employers) page.
uncertainty: The page names 'employers located in Pennsylvania'. It does not say whether an out-of-state employer must withhold. That gap is why the Earnings Tax exists.
designImplication: For most employees the Wage Tax is invisible: the employer withholds it and the employee files nothing.

claim: For City taxes other than Real Estate and Liquor tax, interest is 9% a year (0.75% of the unpaid balance per month) in 2025 and 2026. Penalty is 1.25% per month, unchanged since 1 January 2014. There is no separate failure-to-file fee: the monthly penalty is the late charge. An extension to file does not extend the time to pay.
sourceDate: page undated; accessed 2026-10-11; rates per calendar year
establishes: Philadelphia Revenue: 'For calendar year 2026 ... interest is charged at the rate of 9% per year, 0.75% of the unpaid balance per month'; 'Penalty is currently charged at the rate of 1.25% per month'.
uncertainty: Penalty cap: NOT FOUND (none stated on the page). 2027 interest: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Philadelphia's late charge grows each month (0.75% interest plus 1.25% penalty, about 2% a month), with no published cap.

claim: Revenue offers payment agreements for business taxes, School Income Tax and Earnings Tax. All require an 'affordable down payment' and that current taxes also be filed and paid. Preferred applicants can get up to 60 months with maximum penalty discounts. Standard applicants can get up to 48 months with a smaller discount. Shorter agreements mean fewer penalties, even zero. On default the person 'must pay accrued interest and penalty charges, and you may face legal action and fines.'
establishes: Philadelphia Revenue payment agreement page.
uncertainty: The down payment amount is NOT FOUND (only an 'agreement calculator' is referenced). The page does not say whether interest continues during an agreement.
designImplication: A Philadelphia plan can run for years and cut penalties. Default restores them.

claim: After a bill becomes past due, Revenue sends bills. If its own efforts fail, the debt is referred to outside collection agencies or law firms, which may add fees and may sue. Liens on property, and for real estate even a tax sale, are possible.

steps: referral to outside collection agency or law firm (only after Revenue's efforts fail)

establishes: City of Philadelphia article: collection agencies 'will only contact you if the Department of Revenue's efforts to collect your debt have failed'. It mentions 'Liens on your property, or even a tax sale' and additional fees.
uncertainty: No timeline in days was published. The collection fee percentage for income taxes was NOT FOUND. The 18%/6% legal fee and $106.45 lien charge on the interest-and-penalties page apply to Real Estate Tax only.
designImplication: Escalation is city bill, then agency referral, then suit or lien. There are no published day counts, so model them as ordered stages rather than dates.

claim: Residents owe the Wage Tax on all compensation regardless of where they work. Nonresidents owe it only on compensation for work performed in Philadelphia, at the lower nonresident rate. A nonresident whose employer withheld for days worked outside the city can claim a refund by petition. Employees who qualify can also petition for the income-based rate of 1.5%. Non-Pennsylvania residents must attach a signed copy of their state income tax return to qualify for the income-based rate.
establishes: Philadelphia Revenue Wage Tax and Earnings Tax pages: residents owe 'regardless of where they work'. The pages also cover refund petitions for the income-based rate and for work outside Philadelphia.
uncertainty: The income limits for the 1.5% income-based rate were NOT FOUND. The pages read do not state the remote-work rule (work at home for the employer's convenience) in detail.
designImplication: A nonresident's liability depends on where each day was worked, so a nonresident needs a day count. A resident's does not.

claim: The Columbus municipal income tax rate is 2.5% for tax year 2025, on qualifying wages, net profits and other taxable income. Residents are taxed on all income wherever earned. Nonresidents are taxed on income earned in Columbus.
establishes: Columbus Income Tax Division 2025 IR-25 instructions: 'The Columbus tax rate is 2.5%'. The General Income Tax Information page says the same.
uncertainty: No change was found for 2026 or 2027, but no document stating a 2026 or 2027 rate was found either. 2026 and 2027: NOT FOUND, presumed 2.5% with no source.
designImplication: Use 2.5% as the Columbus rate. A Columbus resident's combined municipal tax is always 2.5% (see the credit entry).

claim: Columbus residents pay a total of 2.5% on all income wherever earned. If they pay tax to another city where they work, Columbus gives 100% credit for that tax, up to 2.5%. A resident working in a 2.5%-or-higher city owes Columbus nothing more. A resident working in a lower-rate city owes Columbus the difference.
establishes: Columbus Income Tax Division: 'Columbus provides 100% credit for tax paid up to 2.5%.' Repeated in the 2025 IR-25 instructions.
uncertainty: None.
designImplication: Resident tax = max(0, 2.5% of income - tax paid to the work city, credit capped at 2.5%).

claim: Columbus does not require every resident to file. A return is required if: (1) a resident has Schedule C, E or F income, even at a loss; (2) a nonresident has Schedule C, E (rental only) or F income earned in Columbus; (3) a resident works in a city with a rate below 2.5% and is not withheld 2.5% in total; (4) wages were earned in Columbus but 2.5% was not fully withheld; or (5) a final return is needed to close an account.
establishes: 2025 IR-25 instructions, 'Do I Need to File?' section, extracted from the PDF text.
uncertainty: None on the list.
designImplication: A fully withheld W-2 resident files nothing. The obligation to file arises only from a shortfall or from self-employment or rental income.

claim: Form IR-25 is due April 15, or October 15 for anyone on a federal extension (the extension is automatic). An extension to file is not an extension to pay. Estimated tax is required if the person expects to owe more than $200. The 2026 instalments are due April 15, June 15 and September 15, 2026 and January 15, 2027, each at least 25%.
establishes: IR-25 instructions: 'For most taxpayers, the return is due April 15. If you are on Federal extension, the return is due October 15.'
uncertainty: None.
designImplication: Columbus uses the federal calendar. An unpaid balance after April 15 accrues penalty and interest even when the person is on extension.

claim: Employers withhold Columbus tax on qualifying wages (generally Medicare wages, box 5). Deposits are semi-monthly (within 3 banking days), monthly (within 15 days) or quarterly (by April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31). Under Ohio law (ORC 718.011), an employer need not withhold for a city where the employee worked 20 or fewer days in the calendar year, unless that city is the principal place of work. After day 20 the employer withholds for all later days.
establishes: Columbus General Income Tax Information page (deposit schedule) and the 2025 IR-25 instructions (box 5). ORC 718.011, the 20-day occasional-entrant rule.
uncertainty: The ORC 718.011 version was read through a summary that described it as unchanged since HB 5 (2015).
designImplication: Withholding goes to the work city first. The resident city collects only the remainder, through the resident's own return.

claim: Ohio's uniform municipal law, ORC 718.27, caps late-payment penalties at 15% of income or estimated tax not timely paid, and 50% of withholding not timely remitted. Interest is the federal short-term rate (July of the prior year), rounded, plus 5%. The 2026 rate is 9%. Columbus says late filing costs '$25 per month up to a maximum of $150', and it applies penalty and interest under Columbus City Code 362.10. A notice with penalty and interest is sent after the return is filed.

value.interestFormula: federal short-term rate (July prior year), rounded, + 5%

establishes: ORC 718.27: penalty on income or estimated tax of 'fifteen per cent of the amount not timely paid'; withholding 'not exceeding fifty per cent'. Interest is 'the federal short-term rate, rounded to the nearest whole number per cent, plus five per cent'. Late filing: $25 per month, maximum $150, from the Columbus General Income Tax Information page. 2026 at 9%: RITA news item of 2025-10-17 (https://www.ritaohio.com/Resources/News/ViewNews?gid=eac59b6f-7952-4772-97c0-4c84f90e0d42). 2025 at 10% (.0274% a day): search snippet of the 2024 Columbus IR-25 instructions.
uncertainty: The 9% for 2026 is from RITA, not Columbus, but the statute fixes one formula for every Ohio municipality. The 2025 figure of 10% is from a search snippet, not a document that was read. The Columbus page's line 'Late payment: 50% of the unpaid tax' appears to be the withholding cap, which conflicts with the 15% statutory cap for individuals. The statute summary read did not confirm the $150 cap. 2027: NOT FOUND (Ohio municipalities publish it by 31 October).
designImplication: An individual's late Columbus tax costs at most 15% penalty, plus statutory interest (9% in 2026) and capped late-filing fees. An employer that does not remit withholding risks up to 50%.

claim: Columbus collects its own income tax through the Income Tax Division of the City Auditor. Taxpayers use the city's CRISP portal (crisp.columbus.gov). It is not a member of the Regional Income Tax Agency (RITA). By contract, the Division also collected for the Northern Pickaway County, Prairie Township and Madison Township JEDDs and Grandview Yard in 2025.

value.collector: City of Columbus, City Auditor, Income Tax Division

sourceDate: City of Columbus 2025 Annual Report; RITA member list (https://www.ritaohio.com/municipalities/rita-member-list/) accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Columbus 2025 Annual Report: 'By contract, this Division administered the collection of the municipal income tax for the following municipalities in 2025...'. Columbus does not appear on RITA's published member list, which does include neighbouring Bexley, Grandview Heights and Worthington (checked by text search of the page).
uncertainty: Non-membership in RITA rests on Columbus being absent from RITA's list, plus secondary sources. No official statement saying 'Columbus is not in RITA' was found. A WebFetch summary of the IR-25 instructions claimed RITA collects for Columbus, but a full-text extraction of that PDF contains no mention of RITA, so that claim was rejected.
designImplication: Columbus tax is paid and filed with the city. Suburbs inside or next to Columbus (Bexley, Grandview Heights, Worthington) file through RITA, which is a different collector.

claim: Bills show the Delinquent Section's phone number. Unresolved delinquent assessments are referred to the City Attorney's Claims Section, which sues. In 2025 the Division referred 2,878 cases ($13,640,336), and the Claims Section filed 1,770 new tax cases. Once a judgment is obtained, cases go to outside collection agencies. Delinquent collections in 2025 totalled $8,771,312, of which $2,970,076 came through the agencies.

steps: referral to City Attorney (Claims Section) for civil suit

sourceDate: City of Columbus 2025 Annual Report; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 2025 Annual Report (City Attorney Claims Section and Income Tax Division sections): 'Once a judgment is obtained by Claims Section staff, these cases are sent to the outside collection agencies for collections.'
uncertainty: Timing between stages: NOT FOUND. Payment plans: the Division says taxpayers unable to pay 'may be eligible for assistance', but no terms (length, down payment) were found. NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Columbus escalates through civil suit and judgment, then outside agencies. There is no administrative lien or wage-levy step comparable to NYS.

claim: The Metro Supportive Housing Services (SHS) personal income tax is 1% of Metro taxable income above a threshold. Tax years 2021 to 2025: $125,000 single, $200,000 joint. 2026: $128,000 single, $205,000 joint. 2027: $132,000 single, $211,000 joint. It applies to residents of the Metro district and to nonresidents with income from Metro sources.
sourceDate: page carries news to 2026-07-19; accessed 2026-10-11; thresholds per tax (calendar) year
establishes: City of Portland Revenue Division personal tax page. The 2025 MET-40 instructions confirm 1% and $125,000/$200,000 for 2025.
uncertainty: The 2026 and 2027 thresholds are inflation-indexed values the Revenue Division has published. The page names no indexing ordinance, and it was not read.
designImplication: SHS is a marginal 1% only on income over the threshold, which rises from 2026. A single filer at $130,000 in 2026 owes 1% of $2,000.

claim: The Multnomah County Preschool for All (PFA) personal income tax is 1.5% of Multnomah taxable income over $125,000 single or $200,000 joint, plus an additional 1.5% over $250,000 single or $400,000 joint (3% marginal at the top). A scheduled 0.8-point increase was originally due in 2026, then postponed to 2027. On 27 August 2026 the Board unanimously delayed it again, to 1 January 2028. The rates for 2025, 2026 and 2027 are therefore 1.5% and 3%.
establishes: Multnomah County news release: the Board voted to delay 'a scheduled increase of the Preschool for All marginal income tax by one year'. The 0.8% increase is now effective 1 January 2028. Portland Revenue's personal tax page confirms 'The rate will increase by 0.8% in 2028'.
uncertainty: No source says whether the 0.8 points is added to each tier (making 2.3% and 3.8%) or only to the top. 'Increase by 0.8%' is ambiguous. No source mentions indexing of the PFA thresholds.
designImplication: PFA is two-tier and not indexed. For 2025 to 2027 a single filer pays 1.5% on $125k to $250k and 3% above $250k.

claim: The City of Portland Revenue Division administers both the Metro SHS and the Multnomah PFA personal income taxes. Each needs its own return: MET-40 or MET-40-NP for SHS, and MC-40 or MC-40-NP for PFA. A combined SHS/PFA return is optional. A full-year resident must file if they file an Oregon return with Oregon taxable income over the threshold. Nonresidents and part-year residents file if their income from the jurisdiction is over the threshold.

value.collector: City of Portland Revenue Division (for Metro and Multnomah County)

establishes: Portland Revenue: 'The City of Portland Revenue Division administers the tax on behalf of Metro' and Multnomah County. MET-40 2025 instructions: 'Every full-year resident of Metro who is required to file an Oregon income tax return ... and who reports Oregon taxable income over ... $125,000 using Oregon filing status single ... is required to file'.
uncertainty: How nonresidents source and apportion income was not read in detail.
designImplication: Separate local returns go to the City of Portland, not the Oregon DOR. One person can owe two local taxes (SHS and PFA) to the same collector.

claim: SHS and PFA returns and payments are due April 15. For tax year 2025 that was April 15, 2026. A federal or state extension serves as the local extension to file, but neither Metro nor Multnomah allows an extension of time to pay. Quarterly estimated payments are required: underpayment is penalised unless payments reach 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's.
establishes: MC-40 2025 instructions: 'Multnomah County does not allow an extension of time to pay'. MET-40 2025 instructions: 'Metro does not allow an extension of time to pay your tax.'
uncertainty: The dollar threshold that triggers estimated payments: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Pay by April 15 even when the return is extended.

claim: Since January 2022, employers with a Metro location must withhold SHS tax from employees who work within Metro and earn $200,000 or more in the calendar year. Employees may opt in or out, or set a different amount, on the Metro OPT form (with a PFA equivalent). Employers remit withholding to the Revenue Division on the same schedule as federal and state withholding. W-2 boxes 18 to 20 carry the local withholding.
establishes: Portland Revenue withholding page: 'employers with a Metro location are required to withhold this tax from employees that work within Metro and earn $200,000 or more during the calendar year.'
uncertainty: The excerpt read stated the $200,000 mandatory rule for SHS. Whether PFA has the same mandatory-withholding rule was not confirmed.
designImplication: Below $200,000 in wages, a taxpayer over the $125,000 threshold will usually have nothing withheld and must pay by estimate or at filing.

claim: For SHS and PFA, late filing costs 5% of the unpaid tax, and late payment costs 5% of the unpaid tax, at least $5. Only one of the two applies when both happen. An extra 100% penalty on the unpaid tax of all years applies if the failure to file or pay runs for three or more consecutive years. Underpayment of estimated tax costs 5%. Interest is computed monthly from the original due date to the 15th of the month after payment: 9.0% a year (0.75% a month) for 16 April 2025 to 15 April 2026, and 8.0% (0.667% a month) for 16 April 2026 to 15 April 2027.
sourceDate: interest policy adopted 2026-05-15; MET-40 and MC-40 2025 instructions; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Portland Revenue Tax Administration Policy on interest rates. MET-40 and MC-40 2025 instructions for penalties ('5% of the amount of the unpaid tax' plus '100% of the unpaid tax of all tax years if the failure ... is for three or more consecutive tax years').
uncertainty: The 'only one penalty applies' rule and the $5 minimum come from portland.gov search summaries. Rates after 15 April 2027: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: The penalty is a one-time 5%, not monthly, so interest does the growing. A third consecutive missed year triggers a 100% penalty, which is the largest risk.

claim: The Revenue Division's payment plan policy covers the PFA and SHS personal income taxes. The set-up fee is generally $25, or $50 for a plan over 24 months. The fee is avoided by paying in full within 12 months. The term is up to 12 months, or 24 months when the balance is over $10,000. A plan stops new penalties unless it defaults. Interest continues. A second late payment is a default: the whole balance becomes due and any penalty waiver is revoked. Someone who defaulted within the last 2 years may get a plan only through the City Attorney, with a Confession of Judgment. An account referred to a third-party collection agency can be charged fees of up to 25% of the balance.
establishes: Portland Revenue Tax Administration Policy, Payment Plans: 'A payment plan stops the imposition of additional penalties unless the payment plan is in default.' The 25% agency fee comes from a portland.gov search summary.
uncertainty: The policy sets 24 months as the maximum but also lists a $50 fee for plans 'exceeding 24 months', so there is a contradiction or a discretionary exception. Liens and garnishment: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: A plan freezes penalties but not interest. Collection escalates through agency referral (up to 25%) or a confession of judgment.

claim: Nonresidents and part-year residents owe SHS on income from sources within the Metro district, and PFA on income from Multnomah County sources, when that income is over the thresholds. They file the -NP forms (MET-40-NP, MC-40-NP), which use a flat-rate return.
establishes: Portland Revenue personal tax page (nonresidents and part-year residents with jurisdiction-source income over the thresholds must file). The 2025 MC-40-NP form title reads 'Non-Resident/Part-Year Resident (Flat ...)'.
uncertainty: The sourcing rules (wages by work location, the remote-work treatment) were NOT FOUND in a page read in full.
designImplication: A Vancouver, WA resident commuting into Portland with high wages owes SHS, and PFA if the work is in Multnomah County, on the wages earned there.

claim: Denver's Employee Occupational Privilege Tax (OPT, or 'head tax') is $5.75 per month. It applies to any individual who performs enough services in Denver to receive at least $500 in compensation for a calendar month. Residence does not matter. The employer also pays a separate Business OPT of $4.00 per month per taxable employee, and per owner, partner or manager regardless of earnings.
sourceDate: General Tax Information Booklet, undated (it cites the 5.15% sales tax rate, so it is current); Tax Guide Topic 61 revised 07/17; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Denver Treasury booklet: 'Each taxable employee is liable for the employee OPT, which is withheld by the employer at a rate of $5.75 per month.' 'Employees need not live in Denver nor the business be based within Denver to be liable for the OPT.' Tax Guide Topic 61 (https://www.denvergov.org/content/dam/denvergov/Portals/571/documents/TaxGuide/TaxGuideTopic61_OccupationalPrivilegeTaxes.pdf) has the same figures.
uncertainty: Neither document is dated for 2025, 2026 or 2027. No change was found. A 2026 or 2027 rate: NOT FOUND beyond these undated documents.
designImplication: A flat $69 a year (12 x $5.75) for anyone earning $500 or more a month for work in Denver. It does not scale with income.

claim: The employer withholds the Employee OPT and remits it with the Business OPT on its OPT return. Employers with 10 or more employees file monthly, due the last day of the following month. Employers with fewer than 10 may file quarterly, due April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. An employee files nothing. Individuals, sole proprietors and partnerships without employees may pay annually, by January 31. Someone with more than one Denver employer pays only once: they give secondary employers Form TD269. An employee who works for one employer in two OPT cities pays only where they spend most of their working hours. There is no such exemption against a city that has no OPT.
establishes: Denver Tax Guide Topic 61, 'Occupational Tax Returns' and 'Exemptions' sections, extracted from the PDF text.
uncertainty: The guide dates from 2017. The 2025-era booklet repeats the same filing frequencies.
designImplication: OPT is an employer-remitted payroll deduction. The employee never has a filing event, so model it as a fixed monthly deduction.

claim: A Denver tax return (including the OPT return) filed after the due date owes a penalty of 15% of the tax due or $25, whichever is greater, plus interest at 1% for each month it is past due.
establishes: Denver Treasury booklet, 'Penalties/Interest for Late Filings': 'you must pay a penalty of 15% of the tax due or $25.00, whichever is greater ... interest is due at the rate of 1% for each month'.
uncertainty: These fall on the employer as filer. No penalty rule aimed at the employee was found.
designImplication: On a $5.75 liability the $25 minimum dominates, so a late OPT return costs at least $25.

claim: For business taxes under DRMC Chapter 53 (which includes OPT), Denver issues a 30-Day Demand. If there is no response within 30 days, the amount becomes final and immediately due, and a tax lien attaches to business goods and equipment, which may be distrained. A Distraint Warrant with a Jeopardy Assessment may follow, served by an Enforcement Officer, after which Denver may change the locks, seize assets and auction them.
establishes: Denver Business Tax FAQ, read only as a search-result summary of the official page.
uncertainty: Read through a search summary only. Collection is against the employer. No individual-employee collection process was found. Payment plans: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: For the employee, OPT carries no collection risk. Any enforcement falls on the employer.

claim: Marion County (Indianapolis, county code 49) has a county income tax rate of 2.02%. This is the rate in Departmental Notice #1 effective 1 October 2026, and the county is not marked as changed since the 1 January 2026 notice. Indiana's state rate for 2026 is 2.95%.
establishes: Indiana DOR Departmental Notice #1, extracted from the PDF text: 'Marion 49 0.0202'. Marion carries no asterisk, which the notice uses to mark a change since 1 January 2026.
uncertainty: 2025: not confirmed from a 2025 notice. Since Marion has no change asterisk since January 2026, the rate held through 2026. 2027: NOT FOUND. SEA 1 (2025) restructures local income taxes and lets cities levy their own. Secondary sources (natlawreview, Baker Tilly) gave 2028 for that, and Indiana Capital Chronicle (2026-03-23) reports it was delayed to 2029.
designImplication: For 2026, treat Indianapolis as a flat 2.02% county tax on Indiana AGI-based income. Watch for the restructuring in 2028 or 2029.

claim: Both county of residence and county of principal employment are fixed on 1 January of the tax year. A resident of an Indiana county on 1 January pays that county's rate. Someone who lives out of state on 1 January but whose principal place of work or business is in an Indiana county pays that county's rate. Since 2024, an employer need not withhold Indiana state or county tax for some nonresident employees who work in Indiana 30 days or fewer in the year.

value.outOfStateResident: county of principal work on January 1

establishes: DN #1: 'Both the county of residence and the county of principal business or employment of an individual are determined on Jan. 1 of the calendar year in which the individual's taxable year begins.'
uncertainty: An Indiana resident of another county who works in Marion pays their home county's rate, not Marion's. This is inferred from the 1 January residence rule.
designImplication: County status is a 1 January snapshot. A move during the year does not change the county until next year.

claim: Employers withhold county tax based on the employee's county on 1 January, using Form WH-4. The individual reports county tax on Schedule CT-40 with the state return: IT-40 for residents, IT-40PNR for part-year residents and nonresidents. For tax year 2025 these were due April 15, 2026. IT-9 or a federal 4868 extends filing to November 16, 2026. Interest runs from April 15. Penalty is waived if 90% was paid by April 15 and the rest by the extended date.
establishes: DN #1 (withholding by county of residence on 1 January, WH-4). The 2025 IT-40 booklet for the due date, extension and Schedule CT-40.
uncertainty: The due date and extension facts come from a search-result summary of the official IT-40 booklet. The booklet was not read in full.
designImplication: Marion County tax rides on the state return and state withholding, much like NYC. There is no separate county filing.

claim: Indiana DOR (which also collects county tax) charges a failure-to-pay penalty of 10% of the unpaid tax or $5, whichever is greater. Failure to file, where DOR prepares the return, carries a 20% penalty. Fraud carries 100%. Underpayment of estimated tax is 10% of the underpayment. Interest is 7% for 2026 and 6% for 2027.
sourceDate: page undated; Departmental Notice #3 published September 2026, effective 2027-01-01 (https://www.in.gov/dor/files/reference/dn03.pdf); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Indiana DOR penalties page: 'Failure to pay tax: 10% of the unpaid tax liability or $5.00, whichever is greater'; 'Failure to file a tax return; preparation by DOR: 20% penalty'. DN #3: 'the rate of interest ... for calendar year 2027 will be 6%'.
uncertainty: The 2025 and 2026 interest figures were read from DN #3's historical table, whose PDF text extraction is columnar. They were matched by position (2025 6%, 2026 7%). A search summary also gave 7% for 2026.
designImplication: Late Marion tax costs a one-time 10% plus the state interest rate. There is no separate county penalty.

claim: DOR collects in three stages: a Notice of Proposed Assessment; a Demand Notice if the debt is not paid or protested within 60 days, which allows 20 days to respond; then a tax warrant. The warrant can include collection fees and clerk costs, and goes to the county sheriff, who may garnish wages, levy bank accounts or auction property. Payment plans through INTIME generally need a balance over $100 for individuals and can run up to 36 months for amounts over $5,001.

steps: Demand Notice (after 60 days; 20 days to respond)
Tax warrant (sheriff): garnishment, bank levy, property auction

establishes: Indiana DOR collection stages pages, read via search summary. Payment plans page (https://www.in.gov/dor/i-need-to/make-a-payment/payment-plans/), read directly: 'Generally, the amount of tax due must be more than $100 for individuals'.
uncertainty: The collection stages come from a search summary of DOR pages. The collection fee percentage on warrants was NOT FOUND.
designImplication: County tax debt follows the state process: notice, demand at 60 days, warrant at 80 days, then sheriff garnishment.

claim: Miami levies no local income tax on residents' wages. The Florida Constitution bars any tax on the income of natural persons who are residents or citizens, whether levied by the state 'or under its authority' (beyond amounts creditable against a federal or other-state tax). Local governments levy taxes only under state authority.
sourceDate: Florida Constitution as published by the Florida Senate; accessed 2026-10-11

VII s.5(a), quoted from a search summary of flsenate.gov and FindLaw: 'No tax upon ... the income of natural persons who are residents or citizens of the state shall be levied by the state, or under its authority, in excess of the aggregate of amounts which may be allowed to be credited upon or deducted from any similar tax levied by the United States or any state.'
uncertainty: The text was read through search summaries. That the ban reaches local governments through 'under its authority' is an interpretation, though the Florida Senate's own description supports it.

claim: Chicago levies no income tax on residents' wages. The old Chicago employer 'head tax' was repealed in 2014. Mayor Johnson proposed a new per-employee charge on large employers for 2026, the 'Community Safety Surcharge'. It does not appear on the Department of Finance's list of tax changes effective January 2026 under the 2026 Revenue Ordinance, passed 2025-12-20. In any version it would have been charged to employers, not withheld from employees.

The Social Housing Tax (from 2025) is 5% of each employee's Seattle compensation over $1,000,000.

Nonresidents (permanent home outside DC and fewer than 183 days there) do not file unless claiming a refund of DC tax withheld, on D-40B. Commuters' wages are not taxed by DC.
